consumption

/kun-SUMP-shun/ - the stress falls on SUMP · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Consumption means the act of using up a resource.

The cabin's propane consumption doubles in January, when the little stove never quite goes cold.

Worked Example

When the aquarium replaced its 1980s pumps, the change showed up first in a spreadsheet: electricity consumption down forty percent in a month, enough saved to fund the otter habitat's expansion. The fish noticed nothing. The accountants threw a small party.

Consumption is the exact word for what that spreadsheet tracked, because consumption means the act of using up a resource — the electricity is not borrowed or stored, it is gone. Intake only measures what comes in; consumption is the burn.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

usage: Usage is consumption's plainer, more neutral twin — the meter word for how much is drawn and spent over a period. It states the amount and stops there; consumption adds the economist's sense that a stock is being drawn down, that whatever was used is now gone.

intake: Intake counts what comes in — calories eaten, water drawn in, fuel loaded — measured at the door, before anything is spent. Consumption is the burn on the far side of that door: the resource actually used up. A tank can record a week's intake and a day's consumption.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

conservation: using less on purpose

production: putting resource in rather than drawing it down

Where it sits · how deeply the stock is depleted — use → consumption → exhaustion

use vs. consumption: Use is far lighter than consumption — neutral and often costless, since you use a library card without the library having less, while consumption always draws the stock down.

exhaustion vs. consumption: Exhaustion goes further than consumption — consumption is the steady drawing-down of a stock; exhaustion is the moment the stock is simply gone.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — con-

Prefix — con-: wholly (an intensifier)

Root — sumpt

Root — sumpt: taken (Latin sumere)

Suffix — -ion

Suffix — -ion: the act of

Put it together

Put it together: Con- (wholly) + sumpt- (taken) + -ion (the act of) = the act of taking something up wholly — using it until it is gone. Latin consumere reshapes to consumpt- for the noun, which is why a p appears that consume never had.

Use the root in a new word: sumptuous

Use the root in a new word: sumptuous: Sumptuous means lavish — literally 'taking much': a sumptuous banquet takes a great deal to put on.

Word Choice

neutral / technical

Consumption is the meter word — fuel, power, water, data — and the economist's word for buying and using. Usage is its plainer twin; intake measures only what enters. When the point is that a stock is being used up, consumption says so.
